scope: Focused evidence screen for Japan, Fayyum/Nile, Suzhou/Pingjiang, Otrar/Transoxiana, Mesopotamia and the Indus. The packet records what can and cannot supervise a 1337 local-food carrying-capacity fit; it does not turn administrative or city observations into synthetic labels.

promotion_audit.decision: No new two-sided scale anchor is admitted. The Japan Great Land Register floors remain in the earlier Farris packets as one-sided evidence. Fayyum, Pingjiang, Otrar, Mesopotamia and Indus records provide high-value physical or validation evidence but fail at least one of the local-food, saturation, boundary, trade or shock requirements. All failures are explicit and retained for audit.

records.label: Japan Kamakura Great Land Registers: provincial rice-field floors, not two-sided capacity labels
records.interval_semantics: Farris (2006), Tables 1.1-1.3, converts registered rice acreage into provincial population floors. The resulting Buzen, Noto and other province records are already preserved as one-sided lower-bound packets; the rice-only conversion and a bracketed non-rice sensitivity do not provide a defensible upper endpoint or saturation fraction.
pressure_evidence: Farris (2006), pp. 22-26 and Tables 1.1-1.2, compares Great Land Register field totals with independent estate surveys, establishing a documented local cultivated-food base.
Farris (2006), pp. 29-32, places late Heian/Kamakura demography in a food-limited setting with grain shortages and famines; this is pressure context, not a measured equilibrium fraction.

The register conversion is tied to local rice acreage and a documented dry-field/non-rice sensitivity, so the retained floors are local-food evidence rather than city population or an imported-food total.
shock_flags: registers are 1190-1199 or 1221 while converted values are labelled circa 1280
partial registers and omitted non-rice fields
Mongol invasion/provisioning-zone exposure for Kyushu provinces
no independent province-level saturation fraction
records.trade_dependence: low_to_mixed; local rice and dry fields are documented, but regional exchange is not quantified
records.food_regime: wet rice, dry fields, pulses, livestock, coastal and river fisheries, forest foods
records.boundary_description: Multiple historical Japanese provinces, not one new aggregate boundary. Buzen, Noto and the other province polygons are mapped in the earlier Japan floor packets with CHGIS/EU5 crosswalks.
records.boundary_source: Harvard CHGIS Japan Tokugawa GIS 2004, DOI 10.7910/DVN/2CVTR0
records.boundary_confidence: high for the individual earlier province packets; not applicable to this screen aggregate
records.source_family_independence: Shared documentary source family with the earlier Buzen/Noto and nine-province lower-bound packets; not an independent global scale family.
sources: Farris, Japan's Medieval Population (2006), pp. 22-32, Tables 1.1-1.3: https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/k/img_auth.php/4/47/Farris_2006.pdf#page=23
Farris, Japan's Medieval Population (2006), Table 1.3 and note c: https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/k/img_auth.php/4/47/Farris_2006.pdf#page=32
Harvard CHGIS Japan data page and Tokugawa Japan GIS 2004: https://chgis.fas.harvard.edu/data/japan/
citation_details: Farris (2006), pp. 29-32, Table 1.3 note c: rice-acreage conversion and bracketed non-rice sensitivity.
records.notes: This screen deliberately avoids creating a duplicate location-level label. The earlier province floors remain valid one-sided tests but cannot establish global scale or train a two-sided residual target.

records.label: Fayyum village cadastral survey of 1245: unusually strong physical evidence, no total population interval
records.interval_semantics: Al-Nabulusi's source is a village-by-village fiscal and irrigation survey, not a headcount. Poll-tax entries cover non-Muslims only, and fiscal revenue combines land and trade taxes; no total population, local-food calorie share or equilibrium saturation interval is available.
pressure_evidence: The Rural Society in Medieval Islam project dates the inspection to spring 1245 and describes a first-hand survey of approximately one hundred villages using local tax and irrigation officials.
The project identifies the nahiya as the agricultural unit for allocating land and water and for paying taxes; hamlets share water quotas with mother villages.
The database records land tax, trade taxes, pasture fees, poll tax and livestock-related payments, exposing water and resource allocation but not a population ceiling.
shock_flags: poll-tax values do not count converted Muslims
fiscal quantities are assessed dues, not production or people
village/hamlet boundary reconstruction is not yet an audited EU5 crosswalk
military iqta and Cairo/royal endowment transfers complicate local-food dependence
records.trade_dependence: mixed; the source explicitly combines land-tax and trade-tax revenue
records.food_regime: Nile basin wheat, barley, beans, rice in suitable pockets, livestock, pasture and fisheries under managed irrigation
records.boundary_description: The roughly triangular Fayyum depression and its approximately one hundred surveyed villages; village and hamlet polygons are not equivalent to the coarse EU5 Egypt locations.
records.boundary_source: Rural Society in Medieval Islam, The Villages of the Fayyum project: https://projects.history.qmul.ac.uk/ruralsocietyislam/
records.boundary_confidence: high for the survey's village concept; low for EU5 equivalence
records.source_family_independence: Independent fiscal/irrigation source family; no population label is inferred from its tax amounts.
sources: Rural Society in Medieval Islam, project overview and source description: https://projects.history.qmul.ac.uk/ruralsocietyislam/
Rural Society in Medieval Islam, digital database: https://projects.history.qmul.ac.uk/ruralsocietyislam/database/
Rural Society in Medieval Islam, village and water-rights unit: https://projects.history.qmul.ac.uk/ruralsocietyislam/database/i-1-the-village/
Rapoport and Shahar (eds.), The Villages of the Fayyum (2018), Brepols: https://www.brepols.net/products/IS-9782503578332-1
Saleh and Tirole, Taxing Unwanted Populations (AEA preliminary paper), pp. 37-38: https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2018/preliminary/paper/r6TnkDEA
citation_details: Project overview: spring 1245 inspection, village-by-village agricultural and irrigation observations, approximately one hundred villages.
Database, The Village: nahiya is the agricultural and water-allocation unit; taxes include land/trade, pasture, poll and livestock categories.

Saleh and Tirole (AEA preliminary paper), pp. 37-38: the earliest extant Mamluk cadastres with local-level kharaj per land unit are 1375 and 1477; al-Nabulusi's 1245 data lack total landholding area needed for the same measure.
records.notes: Retain as a high-priority physical feature source and potential future village-level target if a population series and polygon reconstruction are found. Do not convert tax ardabbs or non-Muslim poll heads into a population interval.

records.label: Fayyum 1245 population estimate in Rapoport's quantitative reconstruction
records.interval_semantics: A scholarly review of Rapoport's pp. 71-74 reconstruction reports an extrapolated total of approximately 75,000 people, including approximately 5,000 in Madinat al-Fayyum. This is a model-derived point estimate from tax-register evidence, not an enumerated interval; no uncertainty bounds are invented.
pressure_evidence: Rapoport's reconstruction compares the medieval total with Roman-era figures and argues that the similarity suggests a higher tax burden was not tenable for the local population; this is qualitative pressure evidence, not an independently measured saturation fraction.
The same review describes Chapter 3 as reconstructing cultivated area, irrigation and population size and Chapters 4-5 as estimating subsistence versus commercial agriculture from the tax figures.

The subsistence regime is explicitly wheat-led with barley and fava beans; rice, cotton, flax and sugarcane are treated as commercial crops, so the source contains a route to local-food decomposition but not a completed calorie share.
shock_flags: 75,000 is an extrapolation from fiscal data, not an enumeration
Madinat al-Fayyum urban component is embedded in the total and must be separated from rural catchment capacity
Ayyubid iqta and military obligations may shift food/tax flows
no formal saturation interval or local-food fraction is published in the accessible review
records.trade_dependence: mixed; Rapoport separates subsistence and commercial agriculture, but inter-regional food flows and urban provisioning remain unresolved
records.food_regime: subsistence wheat, barley and fava beans with commercial rice, cotton, flax and sugarcane under Nile irrigation
records.boundary_description: Fayyum province/depression as reconstructed from al-Nabulusi's village register; the approximately 5,000 Madinat al-Fayyum urban estimate must not be treated as surrounding rural capacity.
records.boundary_source: Rapoport, Rural Economy and Tribal Society in Islamic Egypt (2018), pp. 71-74 (population reconstruction), reviewed by EH.Net and IFAO BCAI
records.boundary_confidence: medium for province reconstruction; low for EU5 equivalence
records.source_family_independence: Independent scholarly reconstruction from the al-Nabulusi fiscal source; it is not independent of the Fayyum cadastral packet and is therefore not counted as a separate source family for scale.
sources: Rapoport, Rural Economy and Tribal Society in Islamic Egypt (2018), pp. 71-74 (book record): https://search.worldcat.org/title/1027116407
EH.Net review, Chapters 3-5 and subsistence/commercial crop interpretation: https://eh.net/book_reviews/rural-economy-and-tribal-society-in-islamic-egypt/
IFAO BCAI review, pp. 59-60 and quantitative discussion: https://www.ifao.egnet.net/bcai/34/21/
Saleh and Tirole, Taxing Identity (TSE working paper), pp. 24-26 and 63-68: https://www.tse-fr.eu/sites/default/files/TSE/documents/doc/by/tirole/taxing_identity_010321.pdf
citation_details: IFAO BCAI/secondary review reports Rapoport's extrapolation (pp. 71-74) to approximately 75,000 total, including approximately 5,000 for Madinat al-Fayyum, and notes equivalence to Roman-era values as evidence that a higher tax burden was not tenable.
EH.Net review identifies Chapter 3 as cultivated-area/irrigation/population reconstruction and Chapters 4-5 as subsistence versus commercial agriculture estimates.
Saleh and Tirole (TSE), pp. 24-26, 63-68: Mamluk 1315/1375 cadastral tax transfers are local village data but are fiscal outcomes, not population or capacity labels.
records.notes: This is the strongest newly located numerical Fayyum evidence, but it remains validation-only until the book's exact assumptions, uncertainty, urban exclusion and historical-to-EU5 village crosswalk are independently audited. It should not be promoted from a point estimate to a two-sided Malthusian target merely because the estimate is plausible.

records.label: Pingjiang Lu (Suzhou) 1290 Yuan register: dense irrigated landscape, administrative point only
records.interval_semantics: The Suzhou local-gazetteer history reports 466,158 households and 2,433,700 people for Pingjiang Lu's six counties in Yuan Zhiyuan 27 (1290). This is a single administrative register point, not an uncertainty interval or a Malthusian equilibrium; no defensible lower/upper population bounds are substituted.
pressure_evidence: The six-county Pingjiang Lu aggregate is a large, densely settled rice-and-canal landscape, making it useful as a thriving local-intensive validation case.
Taihu fisheries, canal transport and administrative food transfers are part of the food regime, but their shares and import dependence are not quantified.
No independent land-scarcity, marginal-land, real-wage or famine-sensitivity evidence is resolved to the same six-county boundary, so the observed point cannot establish saturation.
shock_flags: Yuan register is a tax/administrative count and can omit non-registered categories
six-county Pingjiang Lu boundary is not yet matched to EU5 location polygons
Suzhou/Pingjiang is a commercial canal hub with potentially substantial inter-county food redistribution
no local-food share or saturation fraction
records.trade_dependence: high; canal and market redistribution are central to the record and not separable from local production
records.food_regime: irrigated rice, wheat and legumes, Taihu/freshwater fisheries, pigs and canal redistribution
records.boundary_description: Pingjiang Lu, six Yuan counties around Suzhou; not the modern city polygon and not a closed rural-food catchment for EU5.
records.boundary_source: Suzhou Local Gazetteer Office, Suzhou historical population (Yuan Zhiyuan 27): https://dfzb.suzhou.gov.cn/dfzb/szdq/201507/8d3b864be8d247b991dd1524605f7e9b.shtml
records.boundary_confidence: medium for six-county administrative unit; low for EU5 equivalence
records.source_family_independence: Independent administrative-register source family; the population point is not treated as a capacity label.
sources: Suzhou Local Gazetteer Office, Suzhou historical population: https://dfzb.suzhou.gov.cn/dfzb/szdq/201507/8d3b864be8d247b991dd1524605f7e9b.shtml
Yuan administrative population caveats and source transcription context: https://szzy.7lue.cn/read/b8f1737d5285e7014ed3c229289951e7/e8bf9266f4bbf5de9198fd18aca9514b.md
citation_details: Suzhou Local Gazetteer Office: Yuan Zhiyuan 27 (1290), Pingjiang Lu six counties, 466,158 households and 2,433,700 people.
The register is an administrative/tax count; no source supplies a saturation interval at the same boundary.
records.notes: Retain as a thriving/local-intensive validation point. Do not use it to set surrounding land capacity or to fit a regional multiplier; trade and canal redistribution make it unsuitable for the local-food scale anchor contract.

records.label: Otrar oasis 1200-1350 archaeological population estimate and irrigated landscape
records.interval_semantics: Clarke, Sala, Deom and Meseth report an estimated 21,570 people for phase 4 (1200-1350) in Table 2 (p. 263), based on oasis settlement/irrigation reconstruction and a comparison to UNESCO's approximately 20,000 estimate. It is a point estimate for an oasis that includes the major Silk Road town, not a bounded carrying-capacity interval.
pressure_evidence: The study maps a former oasis of approximately 200 km2 with ten large walled towns and fifty small villages, canals, fields and settlement spacing.

The 1200-1350 phase is explicitly reconstructed from irrigation-channel, field, settlement, pottery, radiocarbon and palaeobotanical evidence; the physical water network is useful for the mechanistic allocator.
The authors state that the population values are estimates and that field work was ongoing; no independent evidence shows the 21,570 population was at a Malthusian equilibrium.
shock_flags: Otrar was a powerful Silk Road urban centre and trade hub
Mongol conquest in 1219-1220 and subsequent irrigation-maintenance disruption
oasis boundary and city-to-rural food flows are not resolved
no saturation fraction or local-food share
records.trade_dependence: high; the study itself identifies Otrar as a key Silk Road route settlement bridging trading, farming and pastoralist cultures
records.food_regime: irrigated cereals and horticulture, livestock/pastoralism, riverine floodplain foods and Silk Road exchange
records.boundary_description: Archaeological Otrar oasis near the Syr Darya/Arys confluence; approximately 200 km2 containing the 170 ha Otrar city platform, ten walled towns and fifty small villages.
records.boundary_source: Clarke, Sala, Deom and Meseth, Reconstructing irrigation at Otrar Oasis, Kazakhstan 800-1700AD, pp. 253-263: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/242240137_Reconstructing_irrigation_at_Otrar_Oasis_Kazakhstan_800-1700AD
records.boundary_confidence: high for archaeological oasis footprint; low for EU5 province equivalence
records.source_family_independence: Independent archaeological/hydrological source family; population estimate and physical irrigation reconstruction are retained together but not treated as an equilibrium target.
sources: Clarke, Sala, Deom and Meseth, Reconstructing irrigation at Otrar Oasis, Kazakhstan 800-1700AD, pp. 253-263 and Table 2: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/242240137_Reconstructing_irrigation_at_Otrar_Oasis_Kazakhstan_800-1700AD
Otrar archaeological geospatial dataset: https://rdr.ucl.ac.uk/articles/dataset/Otrar_archaeological_site_digital_geospatial_dataset_2016/11690835
citation_details: pp. 253-254: 200 km2 oasis, ten large walled towns, fifty small villages, 170 ha Otrar city platform and canal-fed satellite settlements.
p. 263, Table 2: phase 4 (1200-1350) population estimate 21,570; authors note estimate/UNESCO comparison and ongoing field work.
records.notes: Use as a dated irrigation-and-settlement validation case. The crosswalk must remain unresolved until the archaeological oasis polygon is intersected with calibrated EU5 geometry; the city/trade-hub rule independently blocks scale training.

records.label: Lower Tigris-Euphrates canal landscape: physical system evidence without a 1337 population interval
records.interval_semantics: Canal/drainage and settlement studies document a productive but maintenance-sensitive alluvial system; they do not provide a mappable, local-food, two-sided 1337 population or carrying-capacity interval.
pressure_evidence: Remote-sensing and archaeological canal studies document water-control infrastructure and settlement change in southern Mesopotamia.
Salinity, drainage and canal-maintenance constraints are directly relevant to physical production effects, but their population consequences are not independently enumerated at a closed boundary.
shock_flags: Mongol conquest and irrigation-maintenance disruption
salinity and drainage uncertainty
broad alluvial/basin boundary does not match an EU5 local catchment
no population interval and no saturation fraction
records.food_regime: gravity-irrigated cereals, dates, legumes, livestock and riverine foods
records.boundary_description: Lower Tigris-Euphrates alluvial canal landscape; no audited historical village boundary is available for EU5 mapping.
records.boundary_source: ETH/archaeological canal landscape collection and Remote Sensing canal studies
records.source_family_independence: Independent physical/archaeological source family; no population value is inferred.
sources: ETH Research Collection, historical southern Mesopotamia irrigation material: https://www.research-collection.ethz.ch/items/a40b0dba-cc4a-490a-8cc3-d82295dca412
Remote Sensing canal-landscape study: https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/10/12/2042
citation_details: The sources establish canals, drainage, settlement and salinity/maintenance relevance, but no closed 1337 population or saturation interval.
records.notes: Use to constrain irrigation reach, water budgets and salinity risk in the mechanistic model only. Do not extrapolate broad Iraq population estimates or city populations to local capacity.

records.label: Indus basin 1200-1350: irrigation capability evidence, no defensible local aggregate anchor
records.interval_semantics: The available historical irrigation and agrarian sources describe village agriculture and later Sultanate canal works, but no independent 1200-1350 population interval is tied to a closed rural boundary with saturation evidence. Basin or national population estimates are excluded.
pressure_evidence: The Cambridge Economic History of India agrarian chapter describes 1200-1500 village-based peasant agriculture and the input requirements of seed, oxen and tools, useful for technology compatibility.

Historical irrigation summaries document Sultanate canal development, but much of the large-scale Doab expansion is fourteenth-century and cannot be silently treated as 1337 infrastructure everywhere.
No mappable rural aggregate with independent land-scarcity, wage, famine-sensitivity or local-food evidence was found for the 1337 Indus basin boundary.
shock_flags: broad Indus basin spans multiple political and ecological systems
Sultanate conquest and post-1337 canal construction alter the technology/date match
modern basin population and irrigation statistics are not historical labels
no saturation fraction or closed historical boundary
records.food_regime: river/floodplain and rainfed cereals, pulses, pastoralism and locally varying irrigation
records.boundary_description: Indus basin and adjacent Punjab/Sindh plains; basin-scale geography is not a historical village or EU5 local-food catchment.
records.boundary_source: Cambridge Economic History of India, Agrarian Economy (1200-1500): https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/cambridge-economic-history-of-india/agrarian-economy/985CB65E8DCD0DD2E5167EF599C0550C
records.source_family_independence: Independent agrarian/irrigation literature; no population target is admitted.
sources: Cambridge Economic History of India, Agrarian Economy (1200-1500): https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/cambridge-economic-history-of-india/agrarian-economy/985CB65E8DCD0DD2E5167EF599C0550C
International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage, The Indus Basin: History of Irrigation, Drainage and Flood Management: https://icid-ciid.org/publication/publication_details/18
India Water Portal, historical irrigation summary: https://prod-qt-images.s3.amazonaws.com/indiawaterportal/import/sites/default/files/iwp2/report_jan2812.pdf
citation_details: Cambridge chapter scope is 1200-1500 agrarian economy, not a population census or carrying-capacity interval.
The irrigation sources are technology/physical inputs only; post-1337 canal works are not back-projected to 1337.
records.notes: Do not use broad Indus or India population reconstructions as training labels. Keep the candidate as a physical-system research queue until a closed rural boundary and independently vetted saturation evidence are found.
